prompt: In an inkgd integration, why must you connect the `loaded` signal and act inside its handler, rather than reading `current_text` on the line right after `create_story()`?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) create_story() builds the story asynchronously — it returns immediately and reports its result later through the `loaded` signal, (2) reading current_text before the signal fires runs against a not-yet-built story, (3) the read-only properties return empty defaults (and push an error) rather than crashing, so the bug looks like 'nothing happened'. Key insight: the signal is the return channel — act when it fires, not on the next line.

prompt: Why does the reference player call `create_story()` via `call_deferred` instead of directly in `_ready()`?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) inkgd installs a runtime autoload (__InkRuntime) when the plugin is enabled, (2) during _ready() that autoload may not be in the scene tree yet, so calling create_story() immediately can fail with nothing on screen, (3) call_deferred waits one frame so the runtime is ready. Key insight: this is the most common inkgd setup error — a lifecycle/timing trap, not a logic bug.

prompt: Describe the repeating 'advance' cycle for playing an ink story once it has loaded: what calls do you make and how do you know when to stop?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) loop while can_continue, calling continue_story() one line at a time and appending each line's RETURN value to the display (NOT reading current_text after continue_story_maximally() — through InkPlayer that returns only the last line), (2) if has_choices, render current_choices[i].text as buttons; on press call choose_choice_index(i) then advance again, (3) the story ends when the loop exits and there are no choices (can_continue false). Key insight: step line-by-line and accumulate returned text; maximal-continue drops all but the last line through InkPlayer.

prompt: A learner writes `btn.text = current_choices[i]` and gets an object representation instead of the choice label. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) current_choices returns choice OBJECTS, not plain strings, (2) each element exposes a .text property holding the label, (3) the fix is btn.text = current_choices[i].text. Key insight: the array holds ink choice objects; .text is the displayable label (choose_choice_index still takes the integer index).

prompt: What does `get_variable("torch_lit")` demonstrate about the relationship between ink and GDScript, and why is that useful?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) it reads the value of an ink global variable from GDScript, (2) proving ink and the engine share one set of variables — ink state is inspectable from game code, (3) usefulness: the game can react to story state (e.g., unlock a door if torch_lit), and set_variable can push state the other way. Key insight: ink isn't a sealed black box — its variables are a shared bus between narrative and game logic.

prompt: Why is reading an ink line's tags (# speaker: Alfoz) a better way to drive a speaker label than matching on the displayed text in GDScript?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) displayed text is a moving target — writers rephrase, fix typos, and translate it, and any change silently breaks a text match with no error, (2) tags travel in a separate, stable channel that survives rewording, (3) it decouples engine logic from prose. Key insight: display text is for humans, the protocol key is for the machine — never make one channel do both jobs.

prompt: Why must a tags-as-commands player use continue_story() in a loop instead of continue_story_maximally()?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) continue_story_maximally() advances through several lines in one call, (2) current_tags then reflects only the LAST line's tags, so the intermediate lines' tags (commands) are lost, (3) single-step continue_story() returns one line and keeps that line's tags in current_tags. Key insight: per-line tag dispatch requires per-line stepping — maximal continue collapses the tags.

prompt: In the tag dispatcher, what happens when the writer types an unrecognized tag like `# speakr: Alfoz` (misspelled)? Why does the design handle it that way?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) the match falls through to the default `_` branch which calls push_warning, (2) it's a no-op, not a crash — the line still displays, (3) ink itself never validates tags, so misspellings fail quietly; the warning is the safety net that surfaces them. Key insight: the protocol has no engine-enforced schema, so a fall-through warning is how you catch typos without breaking playback.

prompt: The dispatcher's _process_tags returns a bool. What does that bool control, and what still happens regardless of its value?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) the bool decides whether the line's TEXT is displayed (false = hidden, from the # hidden tag), (2) the tags' side effects — setting the speaker, playing a sound — run regardless of the return value, (3) this 'side effects always fire, text is gated' rule lets a story fire effects on every line but show only lines that pass a condition. Key insight: it separates 'do the command' from 'show the words'.

prompt: You need to add a portrait-swap command driven from ink. Using the tag protocol, what do you change — and what do you NOT change?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) add one new match branch in the dispatcher for the new key (e.g. 'portrait': _set_portrait(value)), (2) the writer starts adding # portrait: NAME tags to lines, (3) you do NOT edit the runtime loop or any existing handler, and the story file needs no engine-specific code. Key insight: the protocol is a contract — growing the game is one new handler per command, O(1) in content; the story and engine stay decoupled.

prompt: In an ink+Godot game, when would you use an external function versus a variable observer? Give the direction of data flow for each.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) external function = a PULL: ink calls OUT to game logic when the story needs a value or action (a computed price, a dice roll), declared with EXTERNAL and bound with bind_external_function; (2) variable observer = a PUSH: the game reacts when an ink VAR changes, registered with observe_variable so inkgd calls back on every change; (3) they are not interchangeable — an external can't keep a HUD in sync, an observer can't compute a value for the story. Key insight: match the bridge to the direction the data flows (game-needs-from-story vs game-reacts-to-story).

prompt: You bind an external function that spends gold and plays a coin sound. In testing, the sound fires when the player is merely hovering over a choice that would call it, before they pick it. Why, and what fixes it?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) ink evaluates AHEAD to know which choices to show, and it calls external functions during that lookahead; (2) a side-effecting function (spend gold, play sound) therefore fires during the preview, not just on the real call; (3) fix by binding with lookahead_safe = false, so ink only calls it for real (not during lookahead). Key insight: lookahead_safe = true is for PURE functions (safe to call twice); side-effecting externals must be lookahead_safe = false.

prompt: You register a variable observer on `gold` with observe_variable, but the HUD starts blank and only shows a number after the first purchase. Why, and how do you fix it without polling?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) observe_variable fires only when the variable CHANGES, not at registration — so the callback never runs for the current/initial value; (2) the HUD stays blank until gold first changes; (3) fix by seeding the HUD once yourself right after registering — call the handler with the current value, e.g. _on_gold_changed("gold", _ink_player.get_variable("gold")); (4) after that the observer keeps it in sync. Key insight: observers are for CHANGES; you must seed the initial value manually.

prompt: A teammate implements save/load by writing each ink variable to a file individually and reading them back. The player resumes with the right variable values but in the wrong place in the story, and once-only content plays again. What did they miss?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) ink's state is more than its variables — it also includes visit/read COUNTS, the current knot / CALL STACK, and the RNG seed; (2) saving variables alone drops the current position and read counts, so the story resumes at the wrong knot and once-only ('*') content is re-enabled; (3) use get_state() to serialize the WHOLE state as one JSON string and set_state() to restore it. Key insight: save the single whole-state blob, never hand-pick fields.

prompt: Where in the player lifecycle must you call bind_external_function, and why does timing matter?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) bind AFTER create_story() — the story object must exist for the binding to attach to it; (2) bind BEFORE the first continue_story() — so the binding is in place when ink first evaluates a line that calls the external (including during lookahead); (3) in the reference player this is done in _on_story_loaded, before _advance_story() runs. Key insight: the binding must exist by the time ink first calls the function, or you get a missing-binding runtime error.

prompt: In a multi-story ink game, a fact set in one conversation (e.g. 'the player insulted the mayor') must be readable in a different, separate conversation. What pattern handles this, and what is the mechanism?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) a state-bus variable — a flat namespace of VAR flags used as shared cross-story state; (2) one file writes the flag (~ mayor_insulted = true), any other file reads it in a condition ({mayor_insulted}); (3) it replaces bespoke quest/faction/inventory systems with named booleans/integers; (4) at scale one flag can be read by many files (in Ebb, a variable set in one scene is read by more than half the game). Key insight: cross-conversation memory lives on the shared bus, not inside any one story.

prompt: A production ink game often does NOT use ink's get_state() to save a conversation. How does the stateless-per-dialog pattern persist state instead, and why is it worth giving up ink's built-in save?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) the ENGINE owns the state-bus flags in its own store; (2) each conversation creates a FRESH InkPlayer, seeded from the engine's flags with set_variable before the first line, and harvested back with get_variable on exit; (3) benefits: any dialog is enterable in any order, saves are a flat list of flags (trivial to patch on updates), no single ink file is the source of truth; (4) trade-off: no mid-conversation save (use get_state if you need that). Key insight: durable state lives in the engine; ink files are stateless views seeded from it.

prompt: In a hub-and-spoke conversation, why must each spoke divert BACK to the hub instead of the hub looping on itself? What breaks with a self-loop?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) a knot's read count reflects ENTRY, not internal passes; (2) re-entering the hub by a fresh divert (spoke -> hub) advances read counts correctly AND re-evaluates every choice condition, so gated content appears the moment its flag flips; (3) a knot that loops on ITSELF freezes its own read count, so counts and gates never update (the classic bug); (4) this is the sticky-choice + gather discipline from lessons 02/04. Key insight: fresh entry via divert is what makes read counts and gated choices work — never self-loop.

prompt: A developer stores a 'player has the key' fact as a read count inside key_room.ink and checks it from door.ink, which runs as its own fresh story. The door never unlocks. Why, and where should the fact live?
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) a read count inside key_room.ink is LOCAL to that story instance; (2) door.ink is a different, freshly-created story that never entered key_room.ink's knots, so the count it checks is always zero; (3) they tried to make one ink file OWN world state, but ink files are stateless views; (4) the fact must live on the state bus (a VAR the engine owns and seeds into each fresh story). Key insight: ink is not the game — durable facts that cross conversations belong on the engine-owned bus, not inside a single .ink file.

prompt: Ebb runs combat inside ink with no separate combat system. Map each part of a combat turn to the pattern it reuses, and explain how randomness stays testable.
expected_answer: Should mention: (1) a turn is a hub (hub-and-spoke), (2) the player's actions are choices, (3) the resolution is a tag the engine acts on (e.g. # hploss: 2d6) — the tag protocol from lesson 06, (4) whose-turn / turn state is tracked with state-bus variables; (5) ink never sees the dice — the engine rolls behind the tag and writes the result to the bus, which ink reads on the next entry, so the STORY stays deterministic and randomness lives in one place. Key insight: with the boundary right, new systems (combat) are content, not engineering.
